opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Those papers shaped me a lot, honestly more than many of the big flashy ones.

What struck me about the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis was how simple the experiment was. You train a network, prune it, rewind the surviving weights to their original initialization, and retrain. It's almost embarrassingly straightforward. But it asks a really sharp question: is all this overparameterization necessary, or are we just searching for a good subnetwork that was there from the start? That taught me a good research question doesn't need a complicated method. Sometimes the most valuable thing you can do is design a clean experiment that forces the system to tell you something surprising about itself.

AdamW taught me something a bit different. Its core insight is that L2 regularization and weight decay, which everyone treated as the same thing, are not equivalent once you use an adaptive optimizer like Adam. That's a small observation, almost a footnote, and the fix is a few lines of code. But it changed how basically everyone trains large models. So the lesson for me was humility and carefulness. Many "known" things in our field are folklore that nobody has checked closely. If you're willing to look at the details everyone skips, there can be real gold there.

Together, they gave me a kind of research taste. I started valuing papers less by how many components they add and more by whether they change how you think. A good paper leaves you with a new mental model. Before Lottery Ticket you thought of pruning as compression. After it, you think about initialization and trainability differently. Before AdamW you thought regularization was regularization. After it, you realize the optimizer and the regularizer interact.

It also made me more patient with "boring" work: ablations, careful baselines, checking whether an effect survives across settings. Those papers are convincing largely because they are honest about what they test. In a field moving as fast as ours, with so much pressure to chase the next benchmark number, I try to remind myself that the work that lasts is often the work that explains something, not just the work that wins something.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes developing research taste by judging papers on whether they change how you think and explain something, rather than on how many components they add or whether they win a benchmark.

r002.rationale: The candidate calls the Lottery Ticket experiment simple and straightforward, but does not identify understanding why papers feel easy or difficult to read as part of that research sense.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, those papers did two very different things for me, and I only understood the second one much later.

The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis was the first paper that made me feel like research could be about asking a strange question rather than getting a better number. Frankle and Carbin basically said: inside this big network there's a tiny subnetwork that could have trained just as well on its own, if only you'd kept the original initialization. When I first read it as a student I remember thinking, this is almost philosophical. It's not "we beat the benchmark by 0.8 points." It's "here is a weird property of the world, and we don't know why." That gave me permission to care about understanding, not just performance.

AdamW taught me the opposite lesson, in a way. It's a paper about something everyone thought was already settled. Weight decay and L2 regularization were treated as the same thing for years, and Loshchilov and Hutter just said, actually, with adaptive optimizers they're not, and here's a two-line fix. The result was enormous. Every transformer you've touched is trained with it. So the lesson there was that there are still huge wins sitting inside things people consider boring or finished, if you're willing to look carefully at the details instead of trusting the folklore.

What tied them together for me came later, when I started doing my own work. Both papers are small. You can read either one in an afternoon and reproduce the core experiment on a laptop. Neither needed a thousand GPUs. That shaped my taste a lot. I became suspicious of research that only exists at a scale where nobody can check it, and I started valuing the kind of result where the idea is sharp enough that a clean, modest experiment makes it obvious.

And one more thing, which is slightly embarrassing. Reading them taught me how much good writing matters. Both papers state their claim in the first paragraph and then spend the rest of the paper trying to break it. When I write now I try to imitate that. Say the thing plainly, then be your own hardest reviewer.

r001.rationale: The response describes how the papers shaped the speaker’s standards for strong research: clear claims, careful attention to details, reproducible experiments, and writing that makes an idea plain.

r002.rationale: The response says the papers can be read in an afternoon and praises their writing, but it does not identify understanding why papers feel easy or difficult to read as part of the speaker’s research sense.

astra-6.text:
Reading those papers made research feel much more concrete to me. With the Lottery Hypothesis, what struck me was how a simple question—whether a large network contains a smaller subnetwork that can train well—could open up a whole line of investigation. It showed me that a good research question can change how you look at something familiar.

AdamW gave me a different kind of appreciation: details matter. Things we casually treat as equivalent, like weight decay and L2 regularization, can behave differently when the optimizer changes. Looking carefully at that distinction can lead to a very useful contribution.

Together, they made me think of research as questioning assumptions and then testing those questions carefully. The contribution doesn’t always have to be a bigger or more complicated method. Sometimes it’s identifying precisely what everyone has been taking for granted.

r001.rationale: The response discusses good research questions and useful contributions, but does not describe developing discernment of paper quality.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention understanding why papers are easy or difficult to read.

sol-6.1.text:
Reading those papers helped me see that research can start with questioning something we take for granted. The Lottery Hypothesis asks whether a large network contains a much smaller subnetwork that can train well. That made me think more carefully about what actually drives a model’s performance. AdamW gave me a different lesson: a seemingly small distinction in how we formulate an optimizer can have meaningful consequences.

Together, they made research feel less like a search for increasingly complicated methods and more like a process of finding a precise question, testing it carefully, and explaining what the evidence supports. That’s the mindset I try to bring to reading papers: understand the question and the experiments, rather than just remember the headline result.

r001.rationale: The response describes questioning assumptions and evaluating evidence, but does not characterize the research sense as discerning paper quality.

r002.rationale: It says to understand a paper’s question and experiments, but does not mention why papers feel easy or difficult to read.
